title: Bloomberg & Citadel
summary: Problems whose patterns are commonly reported in Bloomberg and Citadel coding interviews, from Easy to Hard. Approximate and hand curated, not an official or verified question list.
lesson:
About this list
- Each problem practices a pattern that candidates commonly describe from Bloomberg and Citadel technical interviews: limit order books, currency exchange graphs, streaming medians and top-k leaderboards, LRU/LFU caches, monotonic stacks and deques, interval/range tracking, and quantitative dynamic programming.
- Problems are grouped Easy, Medium, and Hard so you can warm up on arrays, leaderboards, and stacks before tackling latency-sensitive heaps, caches, and hard DP.
- The selection is approximate. Interview prompts evolve and vary by team, so treat this track as low-latency data-structure and quantitative algorithm practice rather than a prediction of what you will be asked.

What to expect
- Candidates often report data-structure design and streaming problems (order matching, live leaderboards, rolling hit counters, running median, LRU/LFU caches) paired with strict time and space complexity discussions.
- Expect probing questions on exact amortized vs. worst-case latency, tie-breaking (FIFO at equal price, LRU within equal frequency), and numerical or overflow edge cases.
- Monotonic stack/deque problems and stock/interval DP appear regularly as algorithmic rounds.

How to prepare
- Know when to reach for two heaps (`PriorityQueue`), an ordered map (`TreeMap`), or a hash map + doubly linked list, and be ready to compare their per-operation complexity.
- Check every tie-breaker (maker vs. taker price, arrival sequence, equal frequencies) and verify memory cleanup when buckets or price levels become empty.
- Practice monotonic stack/deque templates and state-machine DP for trading/profit problems.
